Orchard register

Orchard notes from the upper valley describe how the growers prune their pear trees in late winter, choosing the outward buds so the crown opens to the light. They mark each row with a painted stake, record the yield of every tree in a bound register, and compare the harvest against the frost dates kept by the parish clerk. Grafting is done in the third week of spring with scions cut from the oldest trees on the slope, and the unions are wrapped in waxed cloth until the new leaves show. The register also lists which varieties keep through the cold months in the stone cellar and which must be pressed for cider before the first hard freeze.

The keeper's ledger

The lighthouse keeper's ledger records every vessel that passed the northern reef between the spring thaw and the first autumn gale. Each entry gives the hour, the heading, the colour of the hull and whether the crew answered the lamp with a signal of their own. Most entries are brief, but a few run to several lines where the keeper describes fog banks rolling in from the strait, a schooner that anchored overnight to wait out a squall, or a fishing fleet that returned with its nets torn and its holds empty. The ledger was kept in a careful hand for eleven seasons, and the later volumes add a column for the barometer, read at dawn and at dusk, so that the weather can be followed alongside the traffic. Historians of the coast have used it to date the decline of the herring trade, to trace the arrival of the first steam tugs, and to reconstruct the route of a mail packet that was lost with all hands in the great storm of the ninth winter. A careful reader can also follow the keeper's own life through its margins: the births of two children, a long illness noted only by a change of handwriting, and the season when an assistant took over the night watch and the entries became shorter, plainer and more exact.
